Stellar evolution tracks (blue lines) for the pre-main-sequence. The nearly vertical curves are Hayashi tracks.
Low-mass stars have nearly vertical evolution tracks until they arrive on the main sequence. For more-massive stars, the Hayashi track bends to the left into the Henyey track . Even more-massive stars are born directly onto the Henyey track.
The end (leftmost point) of every track is labeled with the star's mass in solar masses ( Template:Solar mass ), and represents its position on the main sequence. The red curves labeled in years are isochrones at the given ages. In other words, stars 1 0 5 years old lie along the curve labeled 1 0 5 , and similarly for the other 3 isochrones.
The Hayashi track is a luminosity–temperature relationship obeyed by infant stars of less than Template:Solar mass in the pre-main-sequence phase (PMS phase) of stellar evolution. It is named after Japanese astrophysicist Chushiro Hayashi . On the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram , which plots luminosity against temperature, the track is a nearly vertical curve. After a protostar ends its phase of rapid contraction and becomes a T Tauri star , it is extremely luminous. The star continues to contract, but much more slowly. While slowly contracting, the star follows the Hayashi track downwards, becoming several times less luminous but staying at roughly the same surface temperature, until either a radiative zone develops, at which point the star starts following the Henyey track , or nuclear fusion begins, marking its entry onto the main sequence .
The shape and position of the Hayashi track on the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram depends on the star's mass and chemical composition. For solar-mass stars, the track lies at a temperature of roughly 4000 K. Stars on the track are nearly fully convective and have their opacity dominated by hydrogen ions. Stars less than Template:Solar mass are fully convective even on the main sequence, but their opacity begins to be dominated by Kramers' opacity

Heinrich Rudolf Hertz (22 February 1857 – 1 January 1894) was a German physicist who produced and detected electromagnetic waves in the laboratory, proving Maxwell 's theory, and who died at 36 with a large part of his programme unfinished.
Hertz was a student of Helmholtz in Berlin, and it was Helmholtz who set him the problem of testing Maxwell's theory against its Continental rivals. At Karlsruhe between 1886 and 1889 Hertz built a spark-gap oscillator and a simple loop receiver, generated waves of roughly metre wavelength, and demonstrated in turn their reflection, refraction, polarisation, diffraction and interference. By setting up standing waves against a metal sheet he measured their wavelength and, with the known oscillator frequency, their speed — finding it equal to that of light. Light and radio waves were shown to be the same thing.
In 1887, while working on the spark gaps, Hertz noticed that ultraviolet light falling on the electrodes made the spark easier to produce. He reported the observation carefully and did not pursue it. It was the discovery of the photoelectric effect , whose explanation eighteen years later won Einstein the Nobel Prize.
Hertz also gave Maxwell's theory the form in which it was taught for a generation. Working in parallel with Oliver Heaviside , he reduced Maxwell's twenty-odd quaternion equations to the compact vector set long known as the Maxwell–Hertz equations. His verdict on what the theory was has been quoted ever since: "Maxwell's theory is Maxwell's system of equations."

Hermann Ludwig Ferdinand von Helmholtz (31 August 1821 – 8 September 1894) was a German physician, physiologist and physicist, and one of the last people able to work at the front of several sciences at once. He gave the conservation of energy its first general statement, proved the theorems that govern vortex motion in an ideal fluid, and founded the modern study of vision and hearing.
Trained as an army surgeon because his family could not afford a physics education, Helmholtz published Über die Erhaltung der Kraft ("On the Conservation of Force") in 1847 at the age of twenty-six, arguing that mechanical, thermal, electrical and chemical processes all exchange a single conserved quantity. In physiology he measured the speed of nerve conduction — found to be finite and surprisingly slow, of the order of tens of metres per second — invented the ophthalmoscope in 1851, developed the Young–Helmholtz trichromatic theory of colour vision, and in Die Lehre von den Tonempfindungen (1863) explained musical timbre in terms of harmonic content, introducing the Helmholtz resonator. The Helmholtz free energy is named for him, as is the Kelvin–Helmholtz contraction timescale for stellar energy release by gravitational collapse. He taught Heinrich Hertz , Max Planck , Wilhelm Wien and Michelson .

This article is copied from Wikipedia and gives the mainstream narrative. For the dispute over who created the theory, and the case made on this wiki, see Relativity priority dispute .
The history of special relativity consists of many theoretical results and empirical findings obtained by Albert A. Michelson , Hendrik Lorentz , Henri Poincaré and others. It culminated in the theory of special relativity proposed by Albert Einstein and subsequent work of Max Planck , Hermann Minkowski and others.
Introduction
Although Isaac Newton based his physics on absolute time and space , he also adhered to the principle of relativity of Galileo Galilei . This can be stated as: as far as the laws of mechanics are concerned, all observers in inertial motion are equally privileged, and no preferred state of motion can be attributed to any particular inertial observer. However, as to electromagnetic theory and electrodynamics, during the 19th century the wave theory of light as a disturbance of a "light medium" or Luminiferous ether was widely accepted, the theory reaching its most developed form in the work of James Clerk Maxwell . According to Maxwell's theory, all optical and electrical phenomena propagate through that medium, which suggested that it should be possible to experimentally determine motion relative to the aether.
The failure of any known experiment to detect motion through the aether led Hendrik Lorentz , starting in 1892, to develop a theory of electrodynamics based on an immobile luminiferous aether (about whose material constitution Lorentz didn't speculate), physical length contraction, and a "local time" in which Maxwell's equations retain their form in all inertial frames of reference. Abstract
We present the history of estimates of the temperature of intergalactic space. We begin with the works of Guillaume and Eddington on the temperature of interstellar space due to starlight belonging to our Milky Way galaxy. Then we discuss works relating to cosmic radiation, concentrating on Regener and Nernst. We also discuss Finlay-Freundlich's and Max Born's important research on this topic. Finally, we present the work of Gamow and collaborators. We show that the models based on a Universe in dynamical equilibrium without expansion predicted the 2.7 K temperature prior to and better than models based on the Big Bang.
Overview
Published in Apeiron in July 1995, this paper by André Assis of the State University of Campinas and Marcos Danhoni Neves of the State University of Maringá is a work of historical scholarship rather than of theory. It assembles the estimates of the temperature of intergalactic space made before Penzias and Wilson's 1965 detection, and argues that models of a universe in dynamical equilibrium, without expansion, "predicted the 2.7 K temperature prior to and better than models based on the Big Bang."
The survey runs from Guillaume in 1896 and Eddington in 1926, who computed the temperature a body would reach in equilibrium with the starlight of the Milky Way; through Regener in 1933 and Nernst in 1937, working from the energy density of cosmic rays; through McKellar and Herzberg, who in 1941 measured the excitation of interstellar CN molecules; to Finlay-Freundlich and Max Born in the early 1950s, whose figures came from a tired-light interpretation of the redshift. Against these the authors set the predictions of Gamow and his collaborators.

Holism (from the Greek holos , "all, whole, entire") is the position that a system and its properties must be understood as a whole, and cannot be fully accounted for by decomposing it into parts and treating the parts separately. Its opposite is reductionism .
The term was coined by Jan Christiaan Smuts in Holism and Evolution (1926), who held that wholes are the real factors in the universe and that the tendency to form wholes is a fundamental principle in nature. The word has since been applied very widely — in philosophy of language, where the meaning of a sentence is held to depend on a whole language; in the philosophy of science, where Duhem and Quine argued that a hypothesis is never tested in isolation but only as part of a whole body of theory; and in systems theory, ecology and medicine.
In physics the mainstream position is not straightforwardly reductionist either. Emergent and collective phenomena — superconductivity, phase transitions, spontaneous symmetry breaking — are standard cases in which a system has properties that its constituents do not, and quantum mechanics describes entangled systems by a single state that cannot be factorised into states of the parts.
Holism in natural philosophy
On this wiki holism carries a stronger and more specific meaning than "the whole is more than the sum of its parts". A large part of the material catalogued here holds that the properties of a local object — its inertia, its mass, even its identity as a particle — are constituted by its relations to the rest of the universe , and cannot be assigned to it in isolation. That is a physical claim rather than a methodological preference, and it is one of the points on which the researchers documented here part company with the Standard Model .
Several distinct strands of that claim run through this wiki.

Abstract
Non-velocity redshifts of the brightest OB stars in the Magellanic Clouds are correlated with their evolutionary ages. The Hubble constant ( H 0 ) is the constant of proportionality in Hubble's law, which states that the redshift of a distant galaxy increases in proportion to its distance. It is quoted in kilometres per second per megaparsec, and in standard cosmology it is read as the present-day rate of expansion of the universe.
The redshift–distance relation was published by Edwin Hubble in 1929, building on radial-velocity measurements made by Vesto Slipher from 1912 onward and on Hubble's own Cepheid distances; Georges Lemaître had derived essentially the same relation from theory two years earlier. Hubble's original slope was about 500 km/s/Mpc, which implied an age for the universe smaller than the known age of the Earth — an embarrassment resolved only when the distance scale was repeatedly revised downward over the following decades. Modern values are near 70 km/s/Mpc. The reciprocal of H 0 , the Hubble time, is about 14 billion years for that value, and is the origin of the familiar figure for the age of the universe.
The Hubble tension
There is a real and unresolved conflict here, and it should not be understated. Measurements that build outward from nearby distance indicators — Cepheid variables calibrating Type Ia supernovae, as in the SH0ES programme — give values around 73 km/s/Mpc. Values inferred instead from the angular power spectrum of the Cosmic Microwave Background , notably by the Planck satellite, give about 67 km/s/Mpc. The quoted uncertainties on both are small enough that the discrepancy is several standard deviations, and a decade of work has failed to make it go away. Independent methods — the tip of the red giant branch, gravitational lensing time delays, and more recently JWST observations of Cepheids — have been marshalled on both sides without settling it.

Scientific Theory
Name Hubble's law
Type Observed redshift–distance relation and its disputed interpretation
Author(s) Edwin Hubble (1929); interpretation disputed — see researchers listed below
Keywords Hubble's law, Hubble constant, redshift-distance relation, expanding universe, tired light, Big Bang
Year 1929
Hubble's law is the observed relation that the redshift of a galaxy is proportional to its distance. Discovered by Edwin Hubble in 1929, it is universally presented as the observational foundation of the expanding universe and hence of the Big Bang .
The relation itself is a well-established empirical regularity. What is disputed — and disputed at length in the literature catalogued on this wiki — is the interpretation invariably attached to it: that redshift measures recession velocity, and therefore that the universe is expanding. That step is an assumption added to the observation, not a consequence of it. Notably, Hubble himself never accepted it.
The observation
Hubble found that the spectral lines of more distant galaxies are shifted further toward the red, and that the shift increases in direct proportion to distance. Written as v = H ₀ d , with H ₀ the Hubble constant, the relation is read in standard cosmology as a recession velocity increasing with distance — the signature of uniform expansion, extrapolated backwards to an initial singularity.
Hubble's own doubts
The man whose name the law carries was consistently sceptical of the expansion reading, and grew more so over time. In correspondence with Willem de Sitter in 1931 he deliberately used the phrase "apparent velocities" to keep the empirical relation distinct from its interpretation, adding that "the interpretation, we feel, should be left to you and the very few others who are competent to discuss the matter with authority." The section opens candidly: "Sometimes we want to jump over the troubles." His Extended Electrodynamics imposes a boundary condition at the interface with vacuum, requiring both μ² and its derivative across the boundary to vanish. He proposes to violate it, and identifies two ways.

A hard violation lets μ² itself jump, so the derivative becomes infinite and the equation's left-hand side is infinite rather than zero. He chooses the hard violation, on the grounds that "it is the same order like the use of a point charge but even better because the integral of energy will not turn infinite." The advantage claimed is decisive: "we will get a static model for any particle with any charge, spin, mass, and magnetic moment."
He then rewrites Gauss's theorem for a vector with a jump across an internal surface, finds that the resulting surface terms are proportional to certain scalars that often vanish or integrate to zero by symmetry, and computes the global quantities.

The dispute over his work and the campaign to suppress it became known as "the Velikovsky affair." title: Natural Philosophy Wiki
content_preview:
Inertia is the resistance of a body to any change in its state of motion. It is the content of Newton's first law — a body continues at rest or in uniform straight-line motion unless a force acts on it — and it is quantified by inertial mass through the second law, F = ma .
Newton set out the law in the Principia (1687) against a background of absolute space, and the difficulty has been there ever since: acceleration relative to what ? Newton's rotating-bucket argument treated the answer as absolute space itself. Ernst Mach rejected that in the 1880s and argued that the inertia of a body is determined by its relation to all the other matter in the universe — the water in the bucket knows it is rotating because the fixed stars are there. Einstein named this Mach's principle in 1918 and took it as one of the motivations for general relativity, but the theory as built realises it only partially: it does predict frame dragging by rotating matter, an effect measured by Gravity Probe B and by satellite laser ranging, but it does not derive local inertial frames from the distant mass distribution, and Einstein himself came to regard the principle as not fully implemented.
The equality of inertial and gravitational mass is one of the best-tested facts in physics, confirmed to about one part in 10 15 . What no accepted theory provides is a mechanism : neither general relativity nor the Standard Model says what physically resists acceleration, or why. This is an acknowledged gap and not a manufactured one.

Inertness is a body's resistance to having its state changed — a property of mass, present whether the body moves or not, and in his view simply a synonym for mass. Inertia is a property of motion: it is the kinetic energy a body carries relative to another body, and it exists only relative to that other body and manifests only in collision. Infinite Universe Theory ( IUT ) is the cosmology developed by Glenn Borchardt as the alternative to the Big Bang. It is the cosmological application of neomechanics and of Borchardt's Ten Assumptions of Science , and it holds that the universe is infinite and eternal in both the microscopic and macroscopic directions, has no origin, no edge and no age, and is therefore not a proper subject for cosmogony at all.
The name belongs to both a theory and a book: Borchardt first set the position out in a 2007 paper for the Proceedings of the Natural Philosophy Alliance , and expanded it into the book Infinite Universe Theory in 2017.
The central argument
Borchardt's case does not begin with data but with an assumption, and with the claim that the opposing assumption is equally unprovable and usually unnoticed. Big Bang cosmology presumes a finite universe with an origin; IUT assumes infinity. Neither can be proven. His contention is that physics adopted finity without ever registering that a choice had been made, and that "fundamental assumptions exist as unconscious presuppositions before they are brought into the light of day."
Once infinity is assumed, an origin becomes incoherent — in his phrasing, "it is not possible for the universe not to exist everywhere for all time" — and the assumptions of inseparability and conservation forbid matter or motion coming into being from nothing. Cosmogony, the study of the origin of the universe, is thus not a difficult science but an illegitimate one, having no object.

title: Natural Philosophy Wiki
content_preview:
Infinity is the concept of the unlimited — of a magnitude, a number, a duration or an extension that has no end. In mathematics it is a working object, handled by rules laid down since Cantor and reproduced in every calculus and set-theory course. In physics it is something else: a quantity that has no meter reading, that no experiment returns, and that appears in the equations of the accepted theories in two very different roles. It appears as an idealisation, harmless and convenient — the infinite straight wire, the infinitely massive source, the limit taken as a variable grows without bound. And it appears as a result, where a theory that was supposed to describe something finite produces a divergence instead: the point-mass singularity of general relativity, the moment of the Big Bang , the infinite self-energy of the electron, the infinite energy density of the zero-point field.
Among the researchers documented on this wiki, infinity is contested ground in both directions at once. Many of them hold that physics has wrongly refused an infinity that is real — the infinite extent and infinite age of the universe — while simultaneously tolerating infinities that are not real, the divergences that arise inside its own equations and are then removed by hand. Others take the opposite view on one or both counts, arguing for a finite closed space, or for a lower limit to divisibility below which no infinity of the small exists. What unites the collection is that infinity is not treated here as a technicality. It is treated as the assumption that decides what kind of universe is being described, usually before any observation has been consulted.
Potential and actual infinity
The distinction that runs under most of these disputes is the classical one between potential and actual infinity. Interacting galaxies ( colliding galaxies ) are galaxies whose gravitational fields result in a disturbance of one another. An example of a minor interaction is a satellite galaxy 's disturbing the primary galaxy's spiral arms . An example of a major interaction is a galactic collision, which may lead to a galaxy merger .
Satellite interaction
A giant galaxy interacting with its satellites is common. A satellite's gravity could attract one of the primary's spiral arms , or the secondary satellite's path could coincide with the position of the primary satellite's and so would dive into the primary galaxy (the Sagittarius Dwarf Elliptical Galaxy into the Milky Way being an example of the latter). That can possibly trigger a small amount of star formation . Such orphaned clusters of stars were sometimes referred to as "blue blobs" before they were recognized as stars. [ 1 ]

Intrinsic redshift is the hypothesis that a significant part of the redshift observed in some astronomical objects — particularly quasars — is not caused by cosmological expansion or by motion away from the observer, but is instead a property intrinsic to the object itself. If true, redshift would cease to be a reliable measure of distance, and the distance scale on which modern cosmology and the Big Bang model rest would require fundamental revision.
The hypothesis is most closely associated with the astronomer Halton C Arp , whose observations of apparently connected objects with wildly differing redshifts formed its principal evidence, and with William Tifft , who reported that galaxy redshifts fall into preferred, quantized values. It remains firmly rejected by mainstream astronomy, but is a central topic in the critical-thinkers literature catalogued on this wiki.
The standard interpretation of redshift
In conventional astronomy an object's redshift is understood as the sum of three effects: the cosmological redshift produced by the expansion of space, the Doppler shift due to the object's own motion, and a usually small gravitational redshift. Because the cosmological term dominates at large distances, redshift is used directly as a distance indicator through Hubble's law — the foundation of the extragalactic distance scale. On this view there is no additional, object-specific component, and a high redshift necessarily means a great distance.

Abstract
The search for frame dragging around massive rotating objects such as the Earth is an important test for general relativity and is actively pursued with the LAGEOS and Gravity Probe-B satellites. Within the classical framework, frame dragging is independent of the state (normal or coherent) of the test mass. This was recently challenged by proposing that a large frame-dragging field could be responsible for a reported anomaly of the Cooperpair mass found in Niobium superconductors. In 2003, a test program was initiated at the Austrian Research Centers to investigate this conjecture using sensitive accelerometers and fiber optic gyroscopes in the close vicinity of fast spinning rings at cryogenic temperatures. This paper will discuss the measurements recently obtained with the fiber optic gyroscopes. They show, that the angular velocity applied to the superconductor can indeed be seen on the sensors below a critical temperature. The signal amplitude is about 8 orders of magnitude below the values applied to the ring for the case of clockwise rotation only. Counter-clockwise rotation responses were at least an order of magnitude weaker. The critical temperature for Al and Nb was 16 K and for YBCO around 32 K, which does not coincide with the material's superconducting temperature. The origin and the signature of the observed signals so far is not clear. Our measurements and analysis suggest that the signal cannot be explained by mechanical influence or by carefully monitored magnetic fields surrounding the sensors.

Ionel Dinu (born 1 June 1972) is a Romanian physicist, physics teacher and experimentalist, best known for his underwater experiments with rotating disks and cylinders , which demonstrate a purely mechanical model for magnetic attraction and repulsion.
Dinu's programme is to show that the forces normally attributed to fields acting across empty space are in fact fluid-mechanical effects in a liquid aether : that electrostatic and gravitational attraction correspond to Bjerknes forces , and that magnetic attraction and repulsion occur between vortices . His experiments are offered as the demonstration that action apparently at a distance is in every case transmitted through the intervening liquid.
His rotating-cylinder result was adopted by Robert de Hilster and David de Hilster as the experimental basis for the magnetic component of the Four Universal Motions , where it is named the "Dinu effect" — a name coined by David de Hilster in Principia Mathematica 2 .
The underwater experiments
The experiments are simple enough to be shown on video and are the reason Dinu is cited elsewhere on this wiki. Cylinders (and in other runs, disks) are set rotating while submerged in water, and their mutual behaviour is observed.

Sir Isaac Newton (25 December 1642 – 20 March 1727, Old Style) was an English natural philosopher and mathematician, author of Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica (1687), and the founder of the mechanical description of nature that governed physics for two centuries.
For many of the researchers collected on this wiki, Newton is not a historical figure who was later superseded but the correct starting point . Among them is an identifiable group who make a strong claim — that the universe is Newtonian at every scale — which puts them directly at odds with the physics of the twentieth and twenty-first centuries.
That is not the position of the wiki as a whole. The critical tradition documented here is varied, and Newtonian mechanics is one strand within it rather than a consensus.
This page gives his life briefly and then documents that tradition. The standard biography is exhaustively covered elsewhere; what follows concentrates on what is contested.
Life and work in brief
Newton was born prematurely at Woolsthorpe Manor in Lincolnshire, three months after his father's death. He entered Trinity College, Cambridge in 1661, and it was during the plague years of 1665–67, when the university closed and he returned home, that he laid the foundations of the calculus, of his theory of colour, and of his thinking on gravitation — the period later mythologised through the falling apple.
He became Lucasian Professor of Mathematics at Cambridge in 1669

Ivor Catt (19 December 1935 – 21 June 2025) was a British electronics engineer known both for pioneering work on high-speed digital logic and wafer-scale integration and, more controversially, for a heterodox account of electromagnetism built on the ideas of Oliver Heaviside. He took a B.A. in engineering at Trinity College, Cambridge, published influential work on crosstalk and interconnection delay in digital systems, and patented the wafer-scale integration technique commercialised in the late 1980s by the British company Anamartic. From the late 1970s onwards he argued, chiefly in the pages of Wireless World and its successor Electronics World , that the textbook treatment of electric current, charge and displacement current is incoherent, and he spent four decades pressing the physics establishment for an answer to what became known as the Catt Question.
Biography
Catt was born on 19 December 1935 in Devon, England, and spent part of his childhood on an RAF airbase in Singapore, leaving with his mother and sister shortly before the Japanese invasion of 1942. He did National Service in Germany, won a State Scholarship in mathematics, and then read engineering at Trinity College, Cambridge, taking his B.A. degree.
He married Freda Mansfield in 1959; the couple had one son. He lived for many years in St Albans, Hertfordshire, from where he ran his own publishing imprints and, from the 1990s, an extensive personal website archiving his writings and his correspondence with academic physicists. Catt died on 21 June 2025 at Watford General Hospital, aged 89.

title: Natural Philosophy Wiki
content_preview:
J. Burton
Residence France
Known for Natural philosopher
There are many scientific theories out there. Some of them are mainstream, others are completely out of mainstream. Whatever their appeal however, how are we to know that a given scientific point of view is better or more accurate than another? Every theory has flaws after all, so how can we be sure that we're on the right track? Is there really a "right track"? Hasn't modern science taught us through its so-called "axiomatic method" that all knowledge is by necessity partial and fragmentary? Aren't we then forever subordinated to an arbitrary choice of postulates that will give us arbitrary theories and arbitrary knowledge? Is that what modernity brought us: knowledge as a matter of taste or "elegance" ? Or else, are we missing something?
It is in that context that I'd like to bring in a new understanding of the nature of reality, which explains its structure regardless of the particular postulates that will be used to build on a given scientific theory. I called this endeavor "Absolute Metaphysics", after Kurt Gödel's concept of a process of "clarification of meaning" expressed in his never publicly delivered 1961 lecture "The modern Development Of The Foundations Of Mathematics In The Light Of Philosophy".

Jack Scholze (born March 6, 1958) is an American independent experimenter based in Honolulu, Hawaii, who builds and tests electromagnetic devices in the amateur "free energy" tradition. He documents his work on a personal YouTube channel, where he presents pulse motors, motor-generators, battery chargers, and energy-capture apparatus wound with unconventional coil geometries.
Biography
Scholze lives in Honolulu, Hawaii, and pursues his experimental work outside of the mainstream academic and industrial physics community. He shares his experiments publicly through online video, positioning himself within a wider community of hobbyists and dissident researchers who investigate claims of over-unity and vortex-based energy.
Work
Scholze's experiments center on direct-current and alternating-current pulse motors, motor-generators, battery chargers, and other energy-capture devices. Much of his work explores exotic inductors and inductor winding geometries, including Rodin coils, Starship coils, conical coils, and designs he associates with names such as Powell Abha, Matthews, and Hendershot coils. Many of these coils are toroidal or donut-shaped and carry several separate windings.
His interest in the geometry of inductors draws on "vortex math" ideas popularized by Marko Rodin, in which winding patterns are arranged according to numerical sequences said to concentrate or channel electromagnetic effects. Scholze presents his devices as investigations into whether such geometries can capture or amplify energy, a premise that lies outside established electromagnetic theory. His contributions consist chiefly of self-published demonstrations and build logs rather than peer-reviewed publications.

Jacques Moret-Bailly is a French physicist and retired professor at the Université de Bourgogne in Dijon, France. Originally a specialist in molecular spectroscopy, he is known in dissident cosmology for proposing the CREIL effect (Coherent Raman Effect on Incoherent Light) as a non-Doppler, non-expansion explanation of astronomical redshifts. (He is also listed on this wiki under the spelling "Moret-Bailey".)
Biography
Moret-Bailly spent his career at the Université de Bourgogne (University of Burgundy) in Dijon, where he worked as a professor of physics before retiring. His early research was in molecular spectroscopy. In later work he turned to theoretical optics and its application to astrophysics and cosmology, publishing a long series of papers from the early 2000s onward.
Scientific work
Molecular spectroscopy
Moret-Bailly's original field was molecular spectroscopy, the study of how molecules absorb and emit light. This background in the interaction of light with matter informed his later work on light propagation through low-density gases.
CREIL and alternative redshift
Moret-Bailly is best known for the Coherent Raman Effect on Incoherent Light (CREIL), which he introduced around 2003 as an alternative account of cosmological redshift. He argues that when ordinary (incoherent) light propagates through a very low-pressure gas of excited atomic hydrogen, a coherent Raman-type interaction shifts the light's frequencies toward the red without blurring images or scrambling the order of spectral lines. Because the shift is smooth and image-preserving, he claims it can be mistaken for a Doppler shift or for cosmological expansion.

James Arathoon is a researcher and speaker in the John Chappell Natural Philosophy Society (CNPS) online seminar series, where he has given talks on the foundations of electromagnetism, the interpretation of the Michelson-Morley experiment, the nature of charge and mass, the fine-structure constant, and the history of science and medicine. His work is critical of Special Relativity and of the conceptual foundations that mainstream physics takes for granted, and he draws on the older critical electromagnetic tradition, particularly the writings of the Irish physicist and mathematician Alfred O'Rahilly.
Biography
Little biographical detail about Arathoon is available in public sources. A 1991 undergraduate thesis submitted for a B.Sc. in Geophysical Sciences at the University of Lancaster, Atmospheric Electricity Investigations: Measurement of Atmospheric Conductivity , reporting measurements made with a Gerdien condenser at a weather station near the university, was self-archived under his name on the Internet Archive in 2023. He has presented regularly in the CNPS livestream seminar series since 2023, hosted by Ian Cowan.

Incompatibilities with Special Relativity
Arathoon argues that Special Relativity is not compatible with the ordinary theory of measurement and with dimensional analysis. On this view the relativistic treatment of length and time is not simply a novel but self-consistent account of measurement; rather, it conflicts with the requirements that any coherent system of physical units and dimensions must satisfy. James R. Hofmann is an American historian of science, Professor of Liberal Studies at California State University, Fullerton . He is the author of André-Marie Ampère: Enlightenment and Electrodynamics (Cambridge University Press, 1995), for a long time the only full-length biography of Ampère in English and still the standard one.
He appears on this wiki because Ampère's force law between current elements is among the most argued-over subjects here, and Hofmann is the historian most often relied on for the circumstances in which that law was produced.
André-Marie Ampère: Enlightenment and Electrodynamics
Published in the Cambridge Science Biographies series edited by David Knight, the book sets Ampère's scientific work against the whole of his life: a man with no formal schooling who read his way through his father's library, whose father was guillotined in the Terror, and who held simultaneously to the scientific optimism of the Enlightenment and to a Catholic faith he found difficult. Hofmann treats the mathematics, the chemistry and the electrodynamics together rather than extracting the physics from the life, and gives close attention to how Ampère actually reasoned from experiment to force law.
"The providential timing of scientific discovery" (2026)
Hofmann returned to the subject for the 250th anniversary of Ampère's birth, in "The providential timing of scientific discovery: André-Marie Ampère in 1820", Comptes Rendus — Mécanique 354 , 671–678 (2026), doi:10.5802/crmeca.374 .

James Noel Robb (March 7, 1942 – August 5, 2023) was an American farmer, U.S. Army radar technician, amateur radio operator, and independent researcher from Danville, Kansas. He pursued self-directed investigations in Electromagnetism , Vortex Theory , biophotonics , and Bioenergy , and held the amateur radio callsign KD0CBW .
Biography
Robb was born on March 7, 1942, in Stillwater, Oklahoma, to Noel Neville Robb and Pauline Louise (Hallman) Robb. From an early age he was drawn to science and technology, becoming an avid reader of Popular Mechanics and an enthusiastic builder of science-fair projects.
Drafted into the United States Army the day before his 25th birthday, Robb trained at the U.S. Army Signal School and served in Vietnam for 19 months and 27 days as a specialist in radar technology (military occupational specialty 26D20, GCA Radar R&M). He was honorably discharged on March 5, 1973 with the rank of Specialist.
Returning to Kansas, Robb farmed the family land near Danville, working as a pioneer farmer from 1968 to 2023. He was also a licensed amateur radio operator under the callsign KD0CBW.
Robb died on August 5, 2023, near Danville while storm spotting and checking his rain gauges. A memorial service was held on August 19, 2023 at Pleasant Valley Mennonite Church in Harper, Kansas, with inurnment at Fairview Cemetery, Danville.

Sorensen is a skilled communicator who enjoys speaking to groups about recent developments in complex scientific theories, and who aims to make difficult material understandable for an audience that is scientifically curious but not necessarily steeped in the sciences. Jean-Claude Pecker (10 May 1923 – 20 February 2020) was a French astrophysicist, author and rationalist. He was Professor at the Collège de France from 1964 to 1988 and Director of the Institut d'Astrophysique from 1972 to 1979, and served as General Secretary of the International Astronomical Union from 1967 to 1970 and as Secretary of the International Academy of Humanism. He wrote several books and hundreds of papers on astronomy, astrophysics, cosmology, human rights, pseudoscience, science and society, and the history of astronomy.
His principal research was in solar physics and stellar atmospheres — the textbook Astrophysique Générale , written with Évry Schatzman, was a standard reference for a generation — and it is from that established position that he engaged, from the 1980s onward, with objections to the standard cosmological model.
Cosmological work
Pecker's contribution to the non-standard cosmology literature centres on the redshift . With Jean-Pierre Vigier he developed a tired-light mechanism in which the redshift arises from an interaction between photons carrying a small non-zero rest mass and the matter lying between source and observer, an account set out in " A Possible Tired-Light Mechanism " (1988). He also worked with Toivo Jaakkola on spatial fluctuations in the Hubble constant, and set out his objections to the standard model directly in " Some Critiques of the Big Bang Cosmology " (1997).

Jesse Babcock (born 1915) is an American self-taught theorist associated with the Natural Philosophy community. He is known for an unorthodox cosmological framework he calls the "true suction" theory, which he developed to explain the origin of matter, energy and Gravity outside the framework of mainstream physics.
Biography
Babcock reports having only an eighth-grade formal education, a fact he presents as central to his outlook, arguing that it left him unencumbered by conventional scientific training. By his own account he became interested in perpetual motion as a child before 1923, and at around the age of fifteen concluded that a working perpetual-motion device could not be built until "the secret of the universe" was understood. He states that experiments imagining spring-and-spoke wheel mechanisms convinced him that any purely mechanical arrangement will always balance out, ruling out perpetual motion in practice.
Babcock dates the origin of his theory to 1953. He recounts hearing a radio report that high-frequency sound waves from jet engines were damaging the lungs of ground crews, which led him to reconsider the idea that sound is "nothing." Reflecting on empty space, he concluded that space must be endless and that it is the only source from which anything could arise.
Work
Babcock's central claim is that space itself possesses a dynamic characteristic he terms "true suction," from which all matter and energy originate. In his view "true suction" is not an object or substance but a property of space, and everything that exists ultimately derives from space and this characteristic.

Jim Johnson (born 22 December 1942) is an American writer and editor based in Olympia, Washington, and the managing editor of The Essential Guide to the Electric Universe , the introductory resource hosted on the Thunderbolts Project website.
Work
The Essential Guide grew out of a request made in 2009 by David Talbott to Bob Johnson, for a summary that would give newcomers enough grounding in plasma behaviour to follow Electric Universe arguments without finding them far-fetched. Jim Johnson took on the task of building that summary into a structured online resource, organised to move from familiar material — stellar distances, the aurorae, planetary magnetospheres — through the history of electromagnetic science to a more technical treatment of plasma, with appendices, a glossary and links to video material.
He presented the project at the 18th Natural Philosophy Alliance conference in 2011, in a paper whose interest lies less in its physics than in its frankness about the state of the field it serves. Johnson describes the Electric Universe as a "paradigm" rather than a theory, on the grounds that its ideas "are less than full-blown theory and are still in a very qualitative state of patterns and examples", and that "underlying mathematics is not yet the EU's long suit". He defends that status as a legitimate stage of enquiry by appeal to the qualitative-physics literature in artificial intelligence, particularly Johan de Kleer's work on causal reasoning about circuits, and argues that the task ahead is to deepen the model with quantitative work rather than to defend it as complete.

John B. Miller is an American physicist and astronomer associated with Western Michigan University in Kalamazoo, Michigan. With his collaborator Thomas E Miller he developed the de Sitter redshift interpretation of the redshifts of quasars and galaxies — an account in which cosmological redshift is a gravitational effect of de Sitter spacetime rather than evidence of an expanding universe.
Scientific work
Miller's work addresses one of the puzzles that has long fuelled non-standard views of redshift : quasars at very high redshift appear almost as bright as objects at intermediate redshift, which is difficult to reconcile with the expansion interpretation, in which more distant (higher-redshift) objects should generally appear fainter.
In his 1994 paper " Are Quasars Manifesting a de Sitter Redshift? " Miller proposed that quasar redshifts are a de Sitter redshift — a gravitational redshift arising in de Sitter spacetime, whose asymptotic character causes the redshift to rise very steeply with distance. On this interpretation an object's observed redshift is not a simple measure of recession velocity or distance, and the near-constant apparent brightness of quasars across a wide range of redshifts becomes expected rather than anomalous.
With Thomas E Miller he later extended the analysis to large modern surveys, arguing that under a de Sitter-space interpretation the intrinsic brightness of objects is roughly the same at all redshifts — for instance, that some 95% of Sloan Digital Sky Survey galaxies and quasars fall within a magnitude range of only about 2.8. The John Chappell Natural Philosophy Society ( CNPS ) is a worldwide society of critical thinkers — professors, PhDs, scientists, engineers and interested lay people — who openly question mainstream physics and cosmology and who develop and present alternative theories, philosophies and models. Taking "natural philosophy" in its older and broadest sense, the society covers physics, cosmology, mathematics and the philosophy and history of science, and provides an open forum for serious scientific work that falls outside the accepted paradigm. It is the organization that owns and maintains the Natural Philosophy Wiki on which this article appears, together with the associated World Science Database.
The society describes itself as "a world-wide think-tank of critical thinkers... who openly criticize mainstream physics and cosmology and who propose alternative theory, philosophy, and models." Its members — many of whom have worked together for more than two decades — apply critical thinking to identify what they see as flaws and failures in mainstream science, and to propose new directions in natural philosophy.
Namesake
The society is named in honour of Dr. John E. Chappell Jr. (1933–2002), a historian of science and earth scientist widely regarded as the modern father of the organized "dissident science" movement. Chappell founded the Natural Philosophy Alliance , the CNPS's predecessor, and devoted much of his life to promoting open, scholarly debate of alternatives to accepted physics — motivated in large part by his conviction that Einstein's theory of relativity was mistaken. John M. Hunter is a British researcher in cosmology and gravitation who proposes that the observed expansion of the universe is better understood as a global rescaling of all lengths and physical constants, and that dark energy is an artefact of misreading the relationship between redshift and scale factor.
Work
The rescaling symmetry principle
Hunter's central proposal, set out in " The Rescaling Symmetry Principle " (2008), is that every length in the universe and every physical constant changes continuously and simultaneously, at a rate governed by the number of length dimensions in the quantity concerned: d Q / Q = aH d t , with H half the Hubble constant. Lengths and the speed of light carry a = 1, Planck's constant 2, the gravitational constant 3, the permittivity of free space −3, while masses, the fine structure constant and the Hubble constant are unchanged.
Because everything changes together, he argues, no local experiment can detect the change — timing light over a fixed distance, or lunar laser ranging for a drift in G , must both return null results. The cosmological redshift, on this account, arises from the changing value of Planck's constant rather than from expanding space.
He reports that the resulting magnitude–redshift relation matches the Type Ia supernova data without invoking dark energy, and that a matter density of one quarter critical follows naturally, with an equation of state parameter of −1.

His own summary of the position, given in the World Science Database record below, is that "dark energy is an illusion created due to the misunderstanding of the relationship between redshift and scale-factor", and that the model reproduces the WMAP5 value of Ω m = 0.249. He has continued to develop the argument in preprints posted to viXra.

Scientific career

John J. Durie is an author known within the dissident-science community for his paper on the telescopic aberration of light, a phenomenon central to long-running disputes over the aether and Einstein's special relativity . He is listed in Jean de Climont's Worldwide List of Dissident Scientists .
Biography
Little verifiable biographical information about John J. Durie is available. He is documented primarily through his 1983 paper on stellar aberration and through his inclusion in de Climont's Worldwide List of Dissident Scientists . His work was circulated within critical-physics circles; the archived copy of his paper was contributed by the dissident physicist Thomas E. Phipps Jr.
Scientific work
Durie's known contribution is his paper "On the Telescopic Aberration of Light," published in the Toth-Maatian Review in January 1983. The paper addresses the aberration of starlight first reported by James Bradley in 1728, in which the observed direction of a star shifts with the Earth's orbital motion. This effect has long been treated as a test discriminating between an aether -based account of light propagation and the relativistic explanation. Durie's analysis engages the classic questions of stellar aberration and ether drag, placing his work among dissident treatments that revisit whether telescopic aberration truly favors special relativity over an aether model.

John Linus O'Sullivan (born 1938) is an Irish-American independent researcher in cosmology and the foundations of physics. Born in Tralee, Ireland, he took up the study of cosmology after retiring from a career in business, and developed a wave-based model in which the electromagnetic field is held to have a duality — much as light has a wave–particle duality — which he presents as a new way of thinking about the structure of the universe. His ideas are his own and are not part of mainstream physics.
Biography
O'Sullivan was born in 1938 in Tralee, County Kerry, Ireland, and has lived in the United States since 1960, settling in Fairfield, Connecticut. After a career in the business world he turned in his retirement to the study of cosmology and physics, working as an independent researcher and publishing his conclusions through the Natural Philosophy community.
Cosmological model
O'Sullivan's central idea is that the electromagnetic field is dual in nature, paralleling the wave–particle duality of the photon. From this starting point he builds an account in which space and matter arise from standing-wave energy: mass, light and gravity are treated as different aspects of the same underlying electromagnetic waves rather than as separate ingredients.
In his 2013 paper " Space and Time " he set out the relationship between space and time in these terms, and in " Electromagnetic Wave Energy and Time " (2015) he developed the theme further, distinguishing a finite energy that carries time — mass-energy linked to light and gravity through "open-ended standing waves" — from an infinite energy that has no time, and arguing that time exists only as the transfer of finite energy. John O'Malley Bockris, an Australian electrochemist, coined the term "hydrogen economy" in the 1970s. Bockris' hydrogen economy describes a system in which hydrogen would be used to transport energy from renewable sources over large distances and store it in large amounts. In 1962, Bockris first proposed a plan to supply US cities with solar-derived energy via hydrogen. In 1971, he published the first article on hydrogen in a referred journal. Bockris published Energy: The Solar-Hydrogen Alternative in 1975, one of the first detailed description of what a solar-hydrogen economy would look like.
Mainstream career
Bockris (1923–2013) was one of the significant figures of twentieth-century electrochemistry, and the great majority of his work is entirely conventional. Born in Johannesburg and raised in England, he took his doctorate at Imperial College London, where he ran a research group in the late 1940s — Martin Fleischmann was among the graduate students who joined its discussions. He moved to the University of Pennsylvania in 1953, then to the Flinders University of South Australia, and to Texas A&M in 1978, where he held a Distinguished Professorship until his retirement in 1997.
His textbook Modern Electrochemistry , written with A. K. N. Reddy and first published in 1970, became one of the discipline's standard works and remains in print. He published several hundred papers across five decades on electrode kinetics, the structure of the electrical double layer, electrocatalysis, corrosion and fuel cells, and supervised a very large number of doctoral students.

Residence Delray Beach, FL, United States
Known for Equivalence Principle , experimental mechanics
Scientific career
Fields Consulting Engineer
John W. McAlister is an American consulting engineer based in Delray Beach, Florida, who has built table-top mechanical experiments intended to test the equivalence of gravitational and inertial mass.
Work
McAlister's first paper, " A Mechanical Test of the Equivalence Principle " (1992), reported an anomalous energy loss in a magnetically suspended body revolving inside a spinning centrifuge, the centrifuge providing a pseudo-gravitational field.
Its successor, " A Special-Case Test of Newton's Second Law of Motion " (2010), was designed to reproduce the effect in a simpler configuration whose retarding forces could be enumerated. A half-kilogram weight falls on a wire over a pulley, drawing a carriage of 1.0 to 4.5 kg along a marble runway on three roller bearings; a microsecond timer records the fall. From thousands of runs over six months he reports an "inertial force index" — the factor by which the carriage's inertia must be increased for the force balance to close — of between 1.030 and 1.118, and concludes that gravitational and inertial mass should not be treated as equal.
The paper's chief merit is that it publishes the full grid of results across eight carriage masses and four drop lengths rather than a single figure, which is what makes the systematics visible: the discrepancy grows as the carriage gets lighter and as the drop gets longer, neither of which a modification of Newton's second law could produce.
He presented the 2010 work at the 17th Natural Philosophy Alliance Conference .
